brief: Heights of N segments; on day d you may lower any chosen segments by 2^(d-1). Find the minimum days so heights become strictly decreasing.
key_idea: After T days each segment can be lowered by any amount in [0, 2^T-1]; so minimise the largest needed reduction and take its bit length.
solution:
1) Go left to right keeping final heights as high as possible: b0=a0, bi=min(ai, b(i-1)-1).
2) Needed reduction di=ai-bi; let mx=max di.
3) Any value <2^T is a sum of distinct powers 1,2,..,2^(T-1), so answer = number of bits of mx (0 if mx=0).
4) Keeping each b as high as possible is optimal: it only loosens the bound for later segments.
5) Use long long; negative heights are fine.
dry_run:
[5,5,5]: b=5, then min(5,4)=4, then min(5,3)=3.
d = 0,1,2 -> mx=2 (binary 10).
Bit length 2 -> answer 2.

brief: Array A of length N with 0<=A[i]<=N; you may increment any element any number of times. List every k for which the MEX can be made exactly k.
key_idea: k is reachable iff for every j<k at least j+1 elements are <= j (Hall's condition); values equal to k can always be pushed above k.
solution:
1) Count cnt[v] for v=0..N.
2) Walk k=0,1,2,...: k is beautiful if the condition holds for all j<k; add k to the answer.
3) Then add cnt[k] to the running prefix; if prefix < k+1, then no larger k can work: stop.
4) Making k absent is always possible by incrementing unused elements past k.
5) The answer is always 0..K for some K<=N; k=0 is always beautiful.

brief: Take elements one by one from the left or right end of the array to form the longest strictly increasing sequence (CF 1157C2, duplicates allowed).
key_idea: Always take the smaller usable end; when both ends are equal, only one side can be used afterwards, so take the longer strictly increasing run from that side.
solution:
1) l=0, r=n-1, last=-inf, ans="".
2) If a[l]!=a[r]: of the ends that are > last, take the smaller one (L or R); if neither is > last, stop.
3) If a[l]==a[r] (and > last): count the strictly increasing run going right from l and the one going left from r; append the longer one entirely (all L or all R) and stop.
4) Stop when l>r. Output the length (and the L/R string).

Ends 2,2 equal: run from left 2,4 (len 2); run from right 2,3,4 (len 3) -> take RRR.
Answer 4: LRRR (1,2,3,4).

brief: Binary string, cash C; flip a bit costs A, swapping ADJACENT bits costs B. Minimise the decimal value with total cost <= C.
key_idea: Only flip 1->0 on the highest 1s; moving a 1 to the right by d positions costs d*B. Try each flip count and spend the rest moving the highest remaining 1s right.
solution:
1) Flipping 0->1 never helps; flips should remove the highest 1s.
2) Plan: try each flip count f (f*A<=C). Flip the f leftmost 1s, then spend the rest (C-f*A)/B adjacent swaps.
3) Swaps: lowering the highest 1 by one place lowers the value the most, so repeatedly move the leftmost 1 that has a 0 right after it one step right. Simulate with care; a 1 stuck behind other 1s cannot move.
4) Compare the final strings lexicographically and output the smallest (mod 1e9+7).
5) No sample is given and it is unclear whether the greedy is exact, so verify against brute force on small cases.
complexity: Roughly O(n * flips + swaps) with simulation; constraints unknown

brief: Binary string S; with CASH coins you can swap any two characters for A coins or flip any character for B coins. Minimise the decimal value and print it mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Try every flip count f; spend the rest on swaps that move the leftmost 1 to the rightmost 0 (while the 1 is left of the 0); then flip the f highest 1s; take the smallest string.
solution:
1) Flips should only turn 1->0, and on the highest 1s. A swap helps only when a 1 is left of a 0.
2) For each f=0..min(ones, CASH/B): s=(CASH-f*B)/A swaps.
3) Do swaps with two pointers: i = leftmost 1, j = rightmost 0, while i<j and swaps remain.
4) Then flip the f leftmost 1s of the result.
5) Keep the lexicographically smallest string (same length, so this is the numeric minimum); output its value mod 1e9+7. Checked against brute force on random small cases.
complexity: O(n * min(ones, CASH/B)) time, O(n) space

brief: Make an array of sea levels strictly decreasing; on day D you may lower any chosen segments by 2^(D-1). Find the minimum number of days.
key_idea: After T days a segment can be lowered by any value in [0, 2^T-1]; greedily keep heights maximal, then answer = bit length of the largest reduction.
solution:
1) b0=L0; bi=min(Li, b(i-1)-1).
2) di=Li-bi; mx=max di.
3) Answer = bits(mx) (0 if already strictly decreasing).
4) |L|<=1e9, so use long long; negative values are fine.

brief: Binary string S, CASH coins; a swap of any two characters costs A, a flip costs B. Minimise the decimal value, output mod 1e9+7 (same as Q0514).
key_idea: Enumerate the flip count; use leftover cash to swap the leftmost 1 with the rightmost 0; flip the highest 1s; keep the minimum.
solution:
1) For f flips (f*B<=CASH, f<=ones): s=(CASH-f*B)/A swaps.
2) Swap the leftmost 1 with the rightmost 0 while the 1 is to the left, up to s times.
3) Flip the f highest remaining 1s.
4) Take the lexicographically smallest result and convert it to a value mod 1e9+7.

brief: Array of 2N numbers; place them so (A0+A1)*(A2+A3)*... is maximum, and find the minimum number of swaps to reach such an arrangement.
key_idea: With a fixed total, the product is largest when the pair sums are balanced: pair the k-th smallest with the k-th largest. Then fixing the pairs is the 'couples holding hands' problem.
solution:
1) Sort a copy; partner(sorted[i]) = sorted[2N-1-i].
2) The order of the pairs does not matter (product is commutative), so only each slot (2i,2i+1) holding a partner pair matters.
3) Greedy as in LC 765: for each slot, if a[2i+1] is not a[2i]'s partner, find the partner (via a position map) and swap it in; count swaps. This is optimal (cycle decomposition).
4) The code assumes distinct values (checked against brute force). With duplicates the pairing is ambiguous and this greedy can overcount, so confirm the statement.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

Slot1=(3,2): ok. Answer 1 (product 5*5=25).

brief: N boxes with strengths S; a ball thrown into box i jumps to i+S[i] (and keeps jumping), and each box it uses loses 1 strength (min 1). Find the minimum balls so all strengths become 1 (mod).
key_idea: Pekora Trampoline (CF 1491C): process left to right; the balls that pass through box i (cur) are free, and you start S[i]-1-cur new balls there; spread their jumps with a difference array.
solution:
1) cur = number of earlier balls that pass through box i (from the difference array).
2) Start need=max(0,S[i]-1-cur) new balls at i; ans+=need.
3) The first S[i]-1 passes jump to i+S, i+S-1, ..., i+2: add +1 on range [i+2, min(n-1,i+S)].
4) Extra passes (cur-(S[i]-1) if positive) leave with strength 1 and go to i+1: add them at i+1 only.
5) Output ans mod 1e9+7.
dry_run:

i=1: cur=0, need=2, ans=3. Output 3.

brief: A deck is a permutation; remove cards in order 1..n. Moving the top card to the bottom, or the bottom card to the top, adds that card's value; you may discard the top card if it is the next one needed. Minimise the total (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: The deck is a circle; whichever way you rotate, card x ends on top and is removed, so the state afterwards is the same. So greedily take min(forward cost, backward cost) at each step, using a BIT for range sums.
solution:
1) Put the values in a BIT at their original positions; keep total = sum of remaining values; top = index of the current top.
2) For x=1..n: fwd = sum of remaining values in the circular range [top, pos[x]) (cards moved top->bottom).
3) The backward cost moves x and every card below it bottom->top = total - fwd.
4) ans += min(fwd, total-fwd); remove x from the BIT; top = pos[x] (the next remaining card after it).
5) Checked against Dijkstra over all states on random small cases.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Design a HashMap with put/get/remove without built-in hash tables (the candidate used linear probing).
key_idea: Open addressing: fixed arrays of keys and values plus a state flag; probe (h+i)%M; deletion leaves a tombstone.
solution:
1) Arrays key[M], val[M], state[M] (0 empty, 1 used, 2 deleted), with M a prime larger than the max number of entries.
2) put: probe from h(k); if the key is found, update it; remember the first tombstone; stop at an empty slot and insert at the tombstone or the empty slot.
3) get: probe until an empty slot; return the value if the key matches in a used slot.
4) remove: find the key and mark the slot deleted (tombstone), so later probes do not stop early.
5) Mention rehashing when the load factor is high.
complexity: O(1) average per operation (low load factor), O(M) space

brief: Count contiguous subarrays of packetHashes whose sum equals targetSum (negative values allowed).
key_idea: Prefix sums: subarray (i,j] sums to T iff P[j]-P[i]=T; count earlier prefixes equal to P[j]-T.

1) cnt[0]=1 (empty prefix).
2) For each element: P+=a; ans+=cnt[P-T]; cnt[P]++.

solution:
1) unordered_map<long long,int> cnt; cnt[0]=1.
2) For x: P+=x; ans+=cnt[P-k]; cnt[P]++.
3) Works with negatives; long long sums.

brief: Count unordered pairs i<j with code[i]==code[j] and j-i<=k.

solution:
1) For j=0..n-1: if j-k-1>=0, decrement cnt[a[j-k-1]] (it left the window).
2) ans += cnt[a[j]]; then cnt[a[j]]++.
3) The window then holds exactly the indices in [j-k, j-1].
4) Use long long for ans.

brief: Count pairs i<j with a[i]==a[j] and j-i<=K (reported N,K up to 1e9, a[i]<=1e5).

1) K=min(K, n-1).
2) Remove a[j-K-1] from the count array as it leaves the window; ans+=cnt[a[j]]; cnt[a[j]]++.
3) a[i]<=1e5, so a plain count array is enough.

solution:

2) For x: P=((P+x)%K+K)%K (keep it non-negative for negative numbers).
3) ans+=cnt[P]; cnt[P]++.
4) Use long long for ans.

brief: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put (hash map + doubly linked list).
key_idea: Hash map from key to a node in a doubly linked list ordered by recency: move to front on access, evict from the back.
solution:
1) The list keeps (key,value) pairs, most recent at the front; the map stores key -> list iterator.
2) get: if missing return -1; else splice the node to the front and return its value.
3) put on an existing key: update the value and splice to front.
4) put on a new key: if size==capacity, erase the back node and its map entry; then push the new node to the front.
5) In an interview, explain why both structures are needed: the map gives O(1) lookup and the list gives O(1) reordering and eviction.

brief: Binary array of length 2n; remove a prefix and a suffix so the rest has equal 0s and 1s; minimise the number removed.

solution:
1) Map 1 -> +1, 0 -> -1; prefix bal; first[0] = 0 (empty prefix).
2) At index i (1-based prefix), if bal was seen before, best = max(best, i - first[bal]); else first[bal]=i.
3) Answer = total length - best (removing everything leaves an empty, balanced array).

brief: Count pairs i<j where a[i]+a[j] is divisible by d and |a[i]-a[j]| is divisible by m.
key_idea: The conditions only depend on residues: need a[i]%m == a[j]%m and a[i]%d == (d - a[j]%d)%d. Count with a map keyed by (a%m, a%d).
solution:
1) For each j: rm=a[j]%m, rd=a[j]%d (normalise negatives with ((x%k)+k)%k).
2) ans += cnt[{rm, (d-rd)%d}].
3) Then cnt[{rm, rd}]++.
4) Use long long; key via pair or rm*d+rd if it fits.

brief: Find the maximum length of a subarray whose sum is >= 0.

2) minL[i]=min(P[0..i]), maxR[j]=max(P[j..n]).
3) i=j=0: if minL[i] <= maxR[j], record j-i and j++; else i++.
4) Answer = best (0 if every element is negative; check whether the problem then wants 0 or -1).

brief: Change the fewest elements so the array is a symmetric mountain: equal ends, rising by exactly 1 per step to the peak, then falling the same way (values may be <= 0).
key_idea: Target at index i is h + min(i, n-1-i); an element is kept iff a[i]-min(i,n-1-i) equals the base h, so pick the most frequent such value.
solution:
1) e_i = min(i, n-1-i).
2) Count the frequencies of key_i = a[i] - e_i.
3) The best base h is the most frequent key (any integer is allowed, since values may be <= 0).
4) Answer = n - max frequency.

brief: Minimum elements to change so the array becomes a symmetric mountain stepping +1 from both equal ends to the peak (values may become <= 0).
key_idea: Normalise each element by its distance to the nearer end; the most common normalised value is the base to keep.

brief: Design an LFU cache with O(1) get and put; ties in frequency are broken by least recently used.
key_idea: key -> (value, freq, iterator); freq -> list of keys in recency order; track minFreq for O(1) eviction.
solution:
1) Maps: kv[key]={val,freq}; pos[key]=iterator into lists[freq]; lists[f] = list of keys, most recent at the front.
2) touch(key): remove it from lists[f]; if lists[f] is empty and f==minFreq, minFreq++; push it to the front of lists[f+1].
3) get: missing -> -1; else touch and return the value.
4) put: if present, update and touch. If not: if full, evict lists[minFreq].back(); insert with freq 1 and set minFreq=1.
5) Capacity 0 means put does nothing.

brief: Meatballs are repeatedly cut and the remainder put back for a number of operations; report the largest remaining meatball. The cutting rule is not stated in the source.

brief: Sort N tasks by time descending (stable), and assign each to the least-loaded of M servers (lowest id on ties); a server that already has k tasks adds D + k*W for the new task. Output the maximum final load.
key_idea: Direct simulation with a min-heap of (load, id) and a per-server task count.
solution:
1) stable_sort the task durations descending.
2) Min-heap of (load, id), all loads 0.
3) For each task D: pop (load,id); load += D + cnt[id]*W; cnt[id]++; push back.
4) Answer = max load over the servers (track it as you go). Use long long.
5) M<=100, so a linear scan also works (O(N*M)).
complexity: O(N log N + N log M) time, O(M) space

brief: For each day output the median of all temperatures so far (average of the two middle values for an even count).
key_idea: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, with sizes kept balanced.
solution:
1) Insert x into lo (max-heap) if x <= lo.top(), else into hi.
2) Rebalance so that lo.size() is hi.size() or hi.size()+1.
3) Median = lo.top() for an odd count, else (lo.top()+hi.top())/2.
4) Sample outputs are integers; print as an integer when exact, or follow the required format.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: n food types; buying type i for the k-th time gives v[i]-(k-1)*d[i] tastiness. Buy at most m items to maximise total tastiness.
key_idea: Each type's gains decrease, so repeatedly take the currently best item from a max-heap and push its next (decayed) value.
solution:
1) Push (v[i], i) for all types.
2) Repeat m times: pop the top t; if t <= 0, stop (buying is optional); total += t; push t - d[i].
3) Greedy is optimal because each type's gain sequence is non-increasing.
4) Use long long.
5) For huge m, binary search a threshold value instead.
complexity: O((n+m) log n) time, O(n) space

brief: For each index i, return the median of temperatures[0..i] (median of a stream).

brief: From an array of 3n elements remove n, keeping order, so that (sum of the first n kept) - (sum of the last n kept) is as large as possible.

brief: Write pseudocode for Bubble Sort and Quick Sort.

2) Quick: quicksort(lo,hi): if lo<hi: p=partition(lo,hi); quicksort(lo,p-1); quicksort(p+1,hi).
3) Partition (Lomuto): pivot=a[hi]; i=lo; for j in lo..hi-1: if a[j]<pivot swap(a[i],a[j]), i++; swap(a[i],a[hi]); return i.
4) Complexities: bubble O(n^2); quick O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst (bad pivots), not stable.
complexity: Bubble O(n^2); Quick O(n log n) avg, O(n^2) worst, O(log n) stack

3) Put the pivot at i; recurse on [lo,i-1] and [i+1,hi].
4) Average O(n log n); worst O(n^2) on sorted input with a fixed pivot; not stable.

brief: Swap two numbers without a temporary variable, then use that swap to sort an array.
key_idea: a^=b; b^=a; a^=b (or a=a+b; b=a-b; a=a-b), plugged into bubble/selection sort; guard against swapping an element with itself.

4) Use it in bubble sort's adjacent swap.

brief: Given a tree as a parent array, count the ways to colour each node white or black so that any two black nodes are at distance >= K (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: dp[v][d] = number of colourings of v's subtree where the nearest black node is at depth d below v (d capped at K = 'none close'); merging children needs a + b' >= K.
solution:
1) Leaf/initial: dp[v][0]=1 (v black), dp[v][K]=1 (v white, no black yet).
2) Merge child c: for each a (current) and b (child), b'=min(b+1,K); skip if a+b' < K (two blacks too close); add to new[min(a,b')].
3) Process nodes in reverse BFS order (avoids deep recursion).
4) Answer = sum of dp[root][*]. K=2 means an independent set; K<=1 gives 2^n.
5) Checked against brute force on random trees.
complexity: O(n * K^2) time, O(n * K) space

brief: A tree with two roots A and B: for each query (U,V), count the nodes in both U's subtree (rooted at A) and V's subtree (rooted at B); queries are decoded online from the previous answer; output the sum mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Every 'subtree under root B' is either an A-subtree, the whole tree, or the whole tree minus one A-subtree, so each answer is an Euler-tour interval overlap.
solution:
1) Root the tree at A; compute an Euler tour tin/tout so that subtree_A(x) = range [tin x, tout x).
2) subtree_B(V): if V==B it is the whole tree; if B is not inside subtree_A(V), it equals subtree_A(V); otherwise it is the whole tree minus subtree_A(c), where c = child of V on the path to B (found by binary lifting from B).
3) Euler ranges are nested or disjoint, so intersections are interval overlaps: answer = |R_U ∩ R_V|, |R_U|, or |R_U| - |R_U ∩ R_c|.
4) Decode each query with the previous answer as the statement says; sum the answers mod 1e9+7.
5) Checked against brute force (without the decoding step).
complexity: O((N+Q) log N) time, O(N log N) space

brief: A tree with roots A and B; each online query (U,V) asks how many nodes lie in U's subtree (rooted at A) and in V's subtree (rooted at B).
key_idea: Root at A with an Euler tour; re-rooting at B changes only V's subtree, which becomes the whole tree minus the A-subtree of V's child toward B when B is below V.
solution:
1) Root the tree at A; compute an Euler tour tin/tout so that subtree_A(x) = range [tin x, tout x).
2) subtree_B(V): if V==B it is the whole tree; if B is not inside subtree_A(V), it equals subtree_A(V); otherwise it is the whole tree minus subtree_A(c), where c = child of V on the path to B (found by binary lifting from B).
3) Euler ranges are nested or disjoint, so intersections are interval overlaps: answer = |R_U ∩ R_V|, |R_U|, or |R_U| - |R_U ∩ R_c|.
4) Decode each query with the previous answer as the statement says; sum the answers mod 1e9+7.
5) Checked against brute force (without the decoding step).

brief: Count pairs i<j with a[i]+a[j]==1.
key_idea: Scan with a count map: add cnt[1-a[j]] before inserting a[j].
solution:
1) unordered_map cnt.
2) For each x: ans += cnt[1-x]; cnt[x]++.
3) Use long long for ans. Sorted two pointers is an alternative (careful with duplicates).

brief: Find the length of the longest subarray with no repeated element.
key_idea: Sliding window with a last-seen map: when a[r] was seen inside the window, move the left end past its previous index.
solution:
1) l=0; last = map value -> latest index.
2) For r: if a[r] is in last and last[a[r]] >= l, set l = last[a[r]]+1.
3) last[a[r]]=r; best=max(best, r-l+1).
4) The same code works on strings (LeetCode 3).
dry_run: Own example: [1,2,3,1,2,4]: r=3 (1 seen at 0) -> l=1; r=4 (2 at 1) -> l=2; r=5 -> window [3,1,2,4] length 4.

brief: N days, some with obligations; cancel at most K obligations to get the longest run of consecutive free days.
key_idea: Longest window with at most K obligation days (like 'max consecutive ones III'); equivalently cancel K consecutive obligations in sorted order.
solution:
1) Sort the obligation days (dedupe).
2) If K >= M, every day is free: answer N.
3) Cancelling a block of K consecutive obligations (in sorted order) is always best. For block i..i+K-1 the free run is from o[i-1]+1 (or day 1) to o[i+K]-1 (or day N).
4) Answer = max run over all blocks (for K=0, the largest gap between obligations).
5) Days are 1..N. This is a sliding window over the obligations; equivalently 'longest run of 1s with at most K zeros flipped' over the day array.
complexity: O(M log M) time (O(N) with the day-array sliding window)
dry_run: Own example: N=10, obligations 3,7, K=1: cancel 3 -> days 1..6 (6); cancel 7 -> days 4..10 (7). Answer 7.

brief: Container With Most Water: choose two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water (the full statement was hidden; LeetCode 11 assumed).
key_idea: Two pointers from the ends; the area is limited by the shorter line, so always move the shorter one inward.
solution:
1) l=0, r=n-1, best=0.
2) area=(r-l)*min(h[l],h[r]); best=max.
3) Move the pointer with the smaller height (moving the taller can never help).
4) Stop when l>=r. Use long long.

brief: Find three numbers whose sum is closest to the target and return that sum (LeetCode 16).
key_idea: Sort; fix i, then use two pointers on the rest, moving toward the target and tracking the closest sum.
solution:
1) Sort; best=a0+a1+a2.
2) For i: l=i+1, r=n-1; s=a[i]+a[l]+a[r].
3) If |s-T| < |best-T|, best=s. If s<T then l++, if s>T then r--, else return s (exact).
4) Use long long.

brief: N boxes in a line each hold a gift type; take exactly K consecutive boxes and maximise the number of distinct types.
key_idea: Fixed-size sliding window with a frequency map and a distinct counter.
solution:
1) Add a[i]: if cnt becomes 1, distinct++.
2) When i >= K, remove a[i-K]: if cnt becomes 0, distinct--.
3) For i >= K-1, best = max(best, distinct).
4) If K > N, handle per statement (take all N).

brief: Find the minimum length of a contiguous subarray that contains every colour 1..C at least once, or -1.
key_idea: Variable sliding window: expand right until all C colours are present, then shrink from the left while still complete.
solution:
1) cnt[1..C], have = number of colours with cnt>0 (ignore values outside 1..C).
2) For each r: add a[r]; while have==C, record r-l+1, then remove a[l++].
3) Output best, or -1 if never complete.
dry_run: N=5, C=3, A=1 2 3 2 1: r=2 -> complete, len 3, remove 1 -> incomplete; r=4 -> {2,3,2,1} complete len 4, shrink -> {3,2,1} len 3. Answer 3.

brief: 'Minimum Withdrawals': reach an amount with the fewest ATM-like withdrawals; only the title is known.
key_idea: Only the title is known. The likely version is Q0940 (take from either end to sum exactly X = longest middle subarray with sum total-X).
solution:
1) The exact rules are not recoverable.
2) If it matches Q0940: target=total-X; find the longest subarray with sum = target (positives -> sliding window); answer = n - len, or -1.
3) If it is denominations, it is coin change: dp[x]=min(dp[x-c]+1).
4) Confirm the statement.
dry_run: Own example (Q0940 reading): [1,1,4,2,3], X=5: total 11, target 6 -> longest middle sum 6 = [1,4] ... [4,2] length 2 or [1,1,4] length 3 -> 5-3 = 2 withdrawals (2+3).

brief: Find all unique triplets that sum to zero (or a target).
key_idea: Sort; fix i; two pointers for the remaining pair; skip duplicates at every level.
solution:
1) Sort.
2) For i: skip if a[i]==a[i-1]; l=i+1, r=n-1.
3) s<0 -> l++; s>0 -> r--; s==0 -> record, then skip duplicates of a[l] and a[r] and move both.
4) Early break when a[i] > 0 (for target 0).
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (besides output)

brief: For every window of length K compute max + min; return the smallest such sum.
key_idea: Two monotonic deques (one decreasing for the max, one increasing for the min) give each window's max and min in O(1) amortised.
solution:
1) maxDq keeps indices with decreasing values; minDq with increasing values.
2) Push i (popping worse elements); pop fronts with index <= i-K.
3) For i >= K-1: best = min(best, a[maxDq.front()] + a[minDq.front()]).
4) Use long long.

brief: Given M obligation days in a calendar, cancel at most K of them to get the longest run of consecutive vacation days.
key_idea: Sort the obligations; cancel K consecutive ones; the run extends from the previous kept obligation to the next kept one.
solution:
1) Sort the obligation days (dedupe).
2) If K >= M, every day is free: answer N.
3) Cancelling a block of K consecutive obligations (in sorted order) is always best. For block i..i+K-1 the free run is from o[i-1]+1 (or day 1) to o[i+K]-1 (or day N).
4) Answer = max run over all blocks (for K=0, the largest gap between obligations).
5) Days are 1..N. This is a sliding window over the obligations; equivalently 'longest run of 1s with at most K zeros flipped' over the day array.
dry_run: Own example: N=10, obligations 2,5,8, K=2: cancel {2,5} -> days 1..7 (7); cancel {5,8} -> days 3..10 (8). Answer 8.

brief: Count the subarrays in which every element appears at most k times.
key_idea: The 'good' property is monotone (sub-subarrays stay good): for each r, find the smallest l with all counts <= k and add r-l+1.
solution:
1) cnt map; l=0.
2) For r: cnt[a[r]]++; while cnt[a[r]] > k: cnt[a[l]]--, l++.
3) ans += r-l+1 (all subarrays ending at r starting at >= l).
4) Use long long (up to n(n+1)/2).

brief: N days with M obligations on given days; cancel up to K obligations to maximise the longest run of consecutive free days.
key_idea: Sort and dedupe the obligation days; cancelling K consecutive ones gives a run from the previous kept obligation+1 to the next kept obligation-1.
solution:
1) Sort the obligation days (dedupe).
2) If K >= M, every day is free: answer N.
3) Cancelling a block of K consecutive obligations (in sorted order) is always best. For block i..i+K-1 the free run is from o[i-1]+1 (or day 1) to o[i+K]-1 (or day N).
4) Answer = max run over all blocks (for K=0, the largest gap between obligations).
5) Days are 1..N. This is a sliding window over the obligations; equivalently 'longest run of 1s with at most K zeros flipped' over the day array.
complexity: O(M log M) time, O(M) space

brief: Merge two sorted arrays using O(1) extra space, so that the first holds the smallest n values and the second the rest, both sorted.
key_idea: Gap (shell-sort) method: compare elements 'gap' apart across the conceptual concatenation and swap if out of order; gap = ceil(gap/2) until 1.
solution:
1) len=n+m; gap=ceil(len/2).
2) For i from 0 while i+gap < len: compare element i and i+gap (map index k to a[k] if k<n else b[k-n]); swap if out of order.
3) If gap==1, stop after that pass; else gap=ceil(gap/2).
4) Simpler alternative: swap a[n-1-i] with b[i] while a[n-1-i] > b[i], then sort both (O((n+m) log)).

brief: An unspecified standard two-pointer / sliding-window question, where wrong window updates cause WA or TLE.
key_idea: No statement: practise the variable-window template (expand right, shrink left while invalid, update the answer at the right moment).
solution:
1) The statement is unknown.
2) Template: for r in 0..n-1: add a[r]; while window invalid: remove a[l++]; update the answer (longest valid) here, or inside the while loop for 'shortest valid'.
3) Common bugs: updating the answer before shrinking; counting with int instead of long long; using a window with negative numbers where the sum is not monotone (use prefix sums plus a hash map instead).
dry_run: Own example (longest subarray with sum <= 5 on [2,1,3,1]): r=2 sum 6 -> drop 2 -> [1,3] len 2; r=3 [1,3,1] sum 5 -> len 3.

brief: Binary string; find the maximum length of a substring that can be made to have equal 0s and 1s using at most k flips.
key_idea: With +1/-1 prefix sums P, window (i,j] works iff |P[j]-P[i]| <= 2k (each flip fixes 2) and the length is even; maximise j-i using the first occurrence of each prefix value plus a range-min over values.
solution:
1) P[0]=0; P[i] += (s[i-1]=='1' ? 1 : -1). first[v] = first index where P equals v.
2) For each j, the best i is the minimum first[v] over v in [P[j]-2k, P[j]+2k] (a sparse table over values gives the range minimum).
3) len=j-i; if len is odd, drop one end (then |diff| <= 2k still holds).
4) Answer = max len. k=0 reduces to the classic first-occurrence map.
5) Length is not monotone in feasibility, so do not binary search on the length. Checked against brute force.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n log n) space
dry_run: Own example: s=1110, k=1: P=0,1,2,3,2. j=4 (P=2): values 0..4 -> first index 0 -> len 4 (3 ones, 1 zero: one flip balances). Answer 4.

brief: Output the maximum of every contiguous window of size k.
key_idea: Deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is the window max; pop the front when it leaves the window.
solution:
1) For i: pop from the back while a[back] <= a[i]; push i.
2) If front <= i-k, pop the front.
3) For i >= k-1, output a[front].
4) Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

brief: Given building heights, compute the total rain water trapped between them.
key_idea: Water at i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) - h[i]; two pointers compute this in O(1) space by always moving the side with the smaller max.
solution:
1) l=0, r=n-1, lm=rm=0.
2) If h[l] < h[r]: lm=max(lm,h[l]); water += lm-h[l]; l++.
3) Else: rm=max(rm,h[r]); water += rm-h[r]; r--.
4) Use long long. Alternatives: prefix/suffix max arrays (O(n) space), or a monotonic stack.

brief: Count subarrays whose product is >= K, in O(n) (positive integers assumed).
key_idea: Complement: total subarrays minus the subarrays with product < K (sliding window, as in LC 713).
solution:
1) Assume a[i] >= 1 (otherwise the window is not monotone; zeros or negatives need separate handling).
2) Count 'less': prod=1, l=0; for r: prod*=a[r]; while prod >= K and l<=r: prod/=a[l++]; less += r-l+1.
3) Answer = n(n+1)/2 - less.
4) Overflow: shrink right after each multiply so prod < K*maxA; or compare in long double / with sums of logs.
dry_run: Own example: [10,5,2,6], K=100: products < 100 count = 8 (as in LC 713); total 10 -> answer 2 ([10,5,2] = 100 and [10,5,2,6]).

brief: Count the windows of length M (out of N integers) where max - min <= C.
key_idea: Fixed-size window max and min with two monotonic deques; check each full window.
solution:
1) Maintain a decreasing deque for the max and an increasing deque for the min.
2) Pop fronts whose index <= i-M.
3) For i >= M-1, count++ if a[max]-a[min] <= C.
4) N up to 1e6: use fast I/O (scanf or ios::sync_with_stdio(false)).

brief: An ATM is an array of positive integers; each withdrawal removes the leftmost or rightmost element. Find the minimum number of withdrawals that sum to exactly X, or -1.
key_idea: The untouched part is a contiguous middle block with sum total-X; maximise its length (all positive -> sliding window).
solution:
1) total = sum; target = total - X. If target < 0, return -1; if target == 0, return n.
2) Sliding window: extend r, shrink l while sum > target; if sum == target, best = max(best, r-l+1).
3) Answer = n - best, or -1 if no window was found.
4) Same as LC 1658 (minimum operations to reduce X to zero).

brief: Maximum sum of a subarray containing at most k distinct values (values may be negative; the empty subarray is allowed).
key_idea: For each right end r the allowed left ends are [L(r), r], with L(r) non-decreasing (two pointers); the best sum is P[r+1] - min P[l] over that range, kept with a monotonic deque.
solution:
1) Prefix sums P.
2) Two pointers: add a[r] to the count map; while distinct > k, remove a[L++].
3) Deque of candidate left indices l (increasing P[l]): push r (popping larger P), pop the front while it is < L.
4) best = max(best, P[r+1] - P[front]); start best at 0 for the empty subarray.
5) Checked against brute force.
dry_run:
A=[1,2,2,3,2,3,5,1,2,1,1], k=2: at r=5 the window is [2,2,3,2,3] (L=1), P[6]-P[1]=13-1=12.
Later windows with 5 contain at most {3,5} or {5,1}: smaller sums. Answer 12.

brief: Find the minimum window of s that contains all characters of t, with multiplicity (LeetCode 76), in O(n).
key_idea: need[] counts from t and a 'missing' counter; expand right; when missing==0, shrink left as far as possible and record the window.
solution:
1) need[c] = count in t; missing = |t|.
2) For r: if need[s[r]] > 0, missing--; then need[s[r]]--.
3) While missing==0: record (l,r); need[s[l]]++; if need[s[l]] > 0, missing++; l++.
4) Return the smallest window, or "".
dry_run: Own example: s=ADOBECODEBANC, t=ABC -> first window ADOBEC (len 6) ... final BANC (len 4).

brief: N prices and K coupons, each saving min(P, D) on one item; choose a window of W items and use at most K coupons in it; maximise the savings (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: The saving per item is s_i=min(P_i,D); for each length-W window take the sum of its K largest s_i, maintained with two multisets.
solution:
1) s_i = min(P_i, D) (all >= 0, so using all K coupons never hurts).
2) Slide a window of length W; 'top' holds the K largest values with their sum, 'rest' holds the others.
3) On add/remove, rebalance: move between the sets so top has K elements and min(top) >= max(rest).
4) best = max over windows; output best % 1e9+7 (compare before taking the mod).
5) The source says 'window of length W' without saying 'exactly'; since savings are >= 0, a full window is never worse.
complexity: O(N log W) time, O(W) space

brief: N prices, K coupons each saving min(P[i], D) on one item; choose a contiguous window of exactly W items and apply at most K coupons in it to maximise the savings (mod 1e9+7).
key_idea: Per item saving s_i=min(P_i,D); the answer is the max over windows of the sum of the K largest s_i, kept with two multisets (top K and rest).
solution:
1) s_i=min(P_i, D).
2) Slide the window; insert the new s_i into top, remove the outgoing one from whichever set holds it.
3) Rebalance: top has K elements and min(top) >= max(rest); keep the running sum of top.
4) Track the max sum (long long; up to 1e5*1e9 fits), then print % 1e9+7.
complexity: O(N log W) time, O(W) space

brief: A good pair is (i<j) with a[i] even and a[j] odd; find the length of the smallest subarray containing at least K good pairs (or -1).
key_idea: The pair count only grows as the window grows, so use two pointers. Adding an odd at the right adds #evens in the window; removing an even at the left removes #odds in the window.
solution:
1) Keep ev, od (counts in the window) and pairs.
2) Add a[r]: if even, ev++; else pairs += ev, od++.
3) While pairs >= K: best = min(best, r-l+1); remove a[l]: if even, pairs -= od, ev--; else od--; l++.
4) Output best or -1. Use long long for pairs (up to n^2/4). Checked against brute force.
dry_run: Own example: [2,4,1,3], K=3: r=2 (odd): pairs=2; r=3: pairs=4 >= 3 -> len 4; remove 2 (even): pairs -= 2 -> 2 < 3. Answer 4.
